# BrewLens

> BrewLens is a free, open-source web interface for browsing, searching, and discovering Homebrew packages (casks and formulae) — a GUI for Homebrew that runs entirely in the browser with no terminal commands required.

BrewLens fetches and parses cask and formula metadata directly from the official Homebrew API (formulae.brew.sh). It is a read-only explorer: it does not install, modify, or manage packages on your machine. Use `brew install --cask <token>` or `brew install <token>` in your terminal to actually install a package.

## Key facts

- Website: https://amit9838.github.io/brewlens/
- Source code: https://github.com/amit9838/brewlens
- License: MIT
- Author: Amit Chaudhary (amit9838)
- Tech stack: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, TanStack Query
- Cost: Free, no account, no tracking of user data (bookmarks and history are stored locally in the browser)
- Data source: Official Homebrew API at https://formulae.brew.sh (cask and formula JSON endpoints)
- Platforms relevant to: macOS (casks and formulae), Linux and Windows Subsystem for Linux (formulae, via Homebrew on Linux / WSL)

## Terminology

- **Cask**: a Homebrew package that installs a macOS GUI application (e.g. `brew install --cask firefox`).
- **Formula**: a Homebrew package that installs a command-line tool or library (e.g. `brew install wget`).
- **Token**: the unique identifier used by Homebrew in install commands and URLs.
- **Brewfile**: a list of packages used to reproduce a Homebrew setup; BrewLens can import and export these.

## What it offers

- Browse and search all Homebrew casks and formulae with instant, keyboard-first search.
- Per-package details: version, description, homepage, install command, download URL, SHA-256 checksum, dependencies, artifacts, deprecation/disable status, and full raw JSON.
- Trending apps based on Homebrew's 30-day install analytics.
- Category browsing (dev tools, AI/LLM, design, media, browsers, productivity, languages, databases, DevOps, networking, VCS).
- Local-only bookmarks, recently viewed history, and a dashboard.
- Brewfile import/export for managing package sets.
- Aggregated Homebrew usage analytics (install counts by period).

## Who uses it

- Developers inspecting formula/cask metadata, versions, and dependencies.
- Security and compliance teams verifying download URLs and SHA-256 checksums.
- Sysadmins auditing packages before deployment.
- Homebrew contributors reviewing package structure before PRs.
- General users discovering macOS apps installable via Homebrew without using the Terminal.
